title: Canned Fish Recipes: Easy Sardine and Canned Salmon Meals
meta_description: Six easy canned fish recipes: sardine toast, salad and pasta, plus canned salmon patties, salad and a skillet, all flavoured with lemon and herbs, not salt.
excerpt: Six easy meals from the cans in your pantry: three sardine recipes and three canned salmon recipes, built on lemon, herbs and vinegar instead of salt.
author: sarah
content:
If there's a stack of sardine and salmon cans at the back of your pantry, you're closer to dinner than you think. Canned fish is already cooked, it keeps in the pantry, and it usually costs less than the fresh counter. The only hard part is knowing what to do once the lid is off.

These canned fish recipes are the ones I'd hand to a friend: three for sardines and three for canned salmon, all built on lemon, herbs and vinegar instead of the salt shaker. Most take about ten minutes. If you'd like to see how a fish meal fits your own calorie and protein numbers, the free PescoDial calculator gives you a starting point from your age, height and weight.

Before You Open the Can

Let me explain why these two cans are worth keeping around. Sardines and salmon are both fatty fish, and both sit on the FDA and EPA "Best Choices" list, the lowest-mercury group. The American Heart Association recommends 2 servings of fish a week, favouring fatty fish, with a serving being 3 ounces cooked. That's the whole case for this page being a set of heart healthy fish recipes. If you want the detail on the fats, I cover it in which fish are high in omega-3.

A handy rule in the kitchen: one small 3.75-ounce can of sardines, drained, holds about 3 1/4 ounces of fish, a little more than one 3-ounce serving. A 5-ounce can of salmon is a generous serving for one, and a tall 14.75-ounce can feeds three or four.

The sodium line

The thing to watch with canned fish is salt. USDA FoodData Central lists canned sardines in oil, drained, at about 260 mg of sodium per 3-ounce serving. Regular canned pink salmon comes in around 325 mg, and the no-salt-added kind around 65 mg. The Dietary Guidelines put the ceiling for the whole day at under 2,300 mg, so most people eating this way pick the lower number when the shelf gives them a choice.

Here's how the recipes below keep the salt down without tasting flat:

  • Buy "no salt added" or "low sodium" cans when you can find them, and compare the sodium line per serving when you can't.
  • Drain the can well before you start.
  • Season with acid and herbs. Lemon juice, lemon zest, vinegar, garlic, black pepper, dill and parsley do the work salt usually does.
  • Go easy on the salty extras. Capers, olives, pickles, mustard, crackers and bread all bring their own sodium, so none of these recipes add salt on top.

If you take medicine: these are everyday foods, but a few medicines are worth a quick conversation first. If you take blood-pressure medicine, the sodium in canned fish, and in the bread or crackers you eat with it, is the part to ask about. If you're on a blood thinner such as warfarin, some of these recipes use parsley and leafy greens, which carry vitamin K, so take that question to your pharmacist, who knows your full medicine list. If you take diabetes medicine, a change in what's on your plate, including the toast, pasta and potatoes here, can change how your blood sugar runs. If you take a statin, ask your doctor or pharmacist before you change how you eat. This is not for everyone. Talk to your doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, diabetes, are pregnant, or take medicine.

Easy Sardine Recipes

Each of these canned sardine recipes starts with one 3.75-ounce can. Sardines packed in olive oil or water both work. If sardines are new to you, start with the toast. It's the gentlest introduction.

1. Lemon sardine toast (serves 1)

  • 1 can sardines, drained
  • 1 slice whole-grain bread, toasted
  • 1 small tomato, sliced
  • Juice of half a lemon
  • Black pepper and a little chopped parsley

Lay the tomato on the toast. Break the sardines into big pieces with a fork and pile them on top. Squeeze the lemon over everything, then finish with pepper and parsley. If you like heat, add a pinch of chili flakes.

2. Sardine and white bean salad (serves 2)

  • 1 can sardines, drained
  • 1 cup no-salt-added canned white beans, rinsed
  • 2 tablespoons finely chopped red onion
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • 1 tablespoon red wine vinegar
  • A handful of chopped parsley, black pepper

Stir the beans, onion, oil and vinegar together in a bowl. Fold in the sardines gently so they stay in chunks. Top with parsley and pepper. It's good right away and better after ten minutes, once the vinegar has soaked in.

3. Garlic and lemon sardine pasta (serves 2)

  • 4 ounces whole-wheat spaghetti
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • 2 cloves garlic, sliced
  • 1 can sardines, drained
  • Zest and juice of 1 lemon
  • 2 big handfuls of arugula or baby spinach

Cook the pasta in unsalted water and save a splash of the cooking water before you drain it. Warm the oil and garlic in a pan over medium-low heat for a minute, then add the sardines and break them up. Toss in the pasta, lemon zest, lemon juice and greens, loosening it with the saved water. Finish with plenty of black pepper.

Canned Salmon Recipes

A quick tip before you start. Canned salmon often comes with the skin and soft bones still in. Both are fine to eat, and the bones mash right into the fish with a fork. They're also where the calcium is. If you'd rather not, buy the boneless, skinless kind.

4. Canned salmon patties (makes 4, serves 2)

  • 1 tall can (14.75 ounces) salmon, drained
  • 1 egg
  • 1/4 cup rolled oats
  • 2 green onions, chopped
  • 1 tablespoon chopped fresh dill, or 1 teaspoon dried
  • Zest of 1 lemon, black pepper
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil for the pan

Mash the salmon in a bowl, then mix in everything except the oil. Shape into 4 patties. If the mix feels loose, let it rest five minutes so the oats can soak up the moisture. Cook in the oil over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until golden and hot through. Serve with a spoonful of plain Greek yogurt stirred with lemon juice and more dill.

5. Salmon salad with yogurt and dill (serves 1)

  • 1 can (5 ounces) salmon, drained
  • 2 tablespoons plain Greek yogurt
  • 1 stalk celery, finely chopped
  • 1 tablespoon lemon juice
  • Fresh or dried dill, black pepper

Flake the salmon and stir in the rest. Eat it on a bed of greens, on cucumber rounds, or tucked into half a whole-grain pita. This one works just as well with canned tuna. If tuna's what you have, how to pick a can of tuna walks through the label.

6. Warm salmon and potato skillet (serves 2)

  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • 1 small onion and 1 bell pepper, diced
  • 2 cups cooked potato, diced (leftover boiled potatoes are perfect)
  • 1 can (5 ounces) salmon, drained
  • 1 tablespoon red wine vinegar or lemon juice
  • Chopped parsley, black pepper

Soften the onion and pepper in the oil over medium heat, about 5 minutes. Add the potato and let it brown without stirring too much. Fold in the salmon in big flakes and warm it for a minute or two. Take the pan off the heat, splash in the vinegar, and finish with parsley and pepper.

Cooking for one

I cook for one most nights, so I know half a can in the fridge is where good intentions go to die. The toast and the salmon salad each use a whole small can. The patties keep well too: cook all four, and tomorrow's lunch is done.

When to Talk to Your Doctor

If you have a known fish allergy, these recipes aren't for you. For everyone else, get checked if you notice any of these:

  • Hives, a rash, swollen lips, itching or tingling in your mouth, or stomach cramps and vomiting soon after eating fish, even if it passes
  • Home blood pressure readings that keep running above the target your doctor gave you
  • New swelling in your ankles or legs, or sudden weight gain over a few days
  • Unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums if you take a blood thinner

Swelling of the tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or feeling faint after eating fish is an emergency. Call 911 or your local emergency number.

The Bottom Line

Two kinds of cans, six meals, no salt shaker. Start with the sardine toast or the salmon salad this week, read the sodium line when you restock, and let lemon and herbs carry the flavour. Simple beats perfect, and a can of fish with a squeeze of lemon counts as dinner.
